meta.description: Master glossary of all vocabulary terms across all 45 skills in Praxis Makes Perfect (Praxis 5403). Deduplicated and sorted alphabetically. These are the key concepts, jargon, and technical terms students must know for the exam.
meta.citationSchema: Each term may include an optional 'citation' string naming the governing statute/regulation or an authoritative source (legal citations, named frameworks, assessment instruments, and measurement standards). General pedagogical terms are intentionally left uncited rather than assigned an invented source. Legal/regulatory citations verified against the eCFR and U.S. Reports, June 2026.

terms.definition: A written plan under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act providing accommodations (e.g., extended time, seating) for students whose disability substantially limits a major life activity; does not require special education eligibility.
terms.citation: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794; 34 C.F.R. Part 104.

terms.definition: Applied Behavior Analysis; a systematic, data-driven approach to understanding and changing behavior using reinforcement, extinction, and environmental modification; foundational to behavioral interventions in schools.
terms.citation: Baer, D. M., Wolf, M. M., & Risley, T. R. (1968), 'Some current dimensions of applied behavior analysis,' Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 1(1), 91–97; Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.).

terms.definition: A single-subject research design that alternates baseline (A) and intervention (B) phases to demonstrate experimental control; behavior should change when intervention is applied and return to baseline when withdrawn.
terms.citation: Single-case experimental design; Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.); Kazdin, A. E. (2011), Single-Case Research Designs (2nd ed.).

terms.definition: A student's demonstrated mastery of academic skills (reading, math, writing) measured by standardized tests; compared to grade-level or national norms in eligibility and progress decisions.
Changes to how instruction or assessment is delivered (e.g., oral testing, extended time) without altering the content or grade-level expectations; preserve validity of the construct being assessed.
The process by which individuals from one culture adopt norms, values, or behaviors of another culture; occurs on a continuum and can produce acculturative stress that affects behavior and learning.
Adverse Childhood Experiences; traumatic events (abuse, neglect, household dysfunction) occurring before age 18 that are linked to long-term negative health, behavioral, and educational outcomes.
terms.citation: Felitti, V. J., et al. (1998), 'Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults: The ACE Study,' American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 14(4), 245–258.

terms.definition: A standardized instrument measuring acquired knowledge and skills in specific academic areas (reading, math, writing); used for eligibility decisions, placement, and progress evaluation.
The first stage of the instructional hierarchy in which the learner is initially learning a skill and accuracy is prioritized over speed; appropriate instructional focus is modeling and feedback.
terms.citation: Instructional hierarchy; Haring, N. G., Lovitt, T. C., Eaton, M. D., & Hansen, C. L. (1978). The Fourth R: Research in the Classroom. Merrill.

terms.definition: Americans with Disabilities Act; a civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against individuals with disabilities in employment, public accommodations, and education; broader than Section 504.
terms.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.

terms.definition: The final stage of the instructional hierarchy in which a student applies a learned skill in novel contexts beyond the original training setting; the most advanced level of skill mastery.
terms.citation: Instructional hierarchy; Haring, N. G., Lovitt, T. C., Eaton, M. D., & Hansen, C. L. (1978). The Fourth R: Research in the Classroom. Merrill.

terms.definition: Skills needed for daily living (communication, self-care, social skills, community use); significantly impaired adaptive behavior is required—along with low IQ—for an intellectual disability diagnosis.
terms.citation: American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) (2021), Intellectual Disability: Definition, Classification, and Systems of Supports (12th ed.). See also Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (Pearson).

terms.definition: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder; a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent, impairing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity present across at least two settings.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Actions taken by school psychologists on behalf of students, families, or the profession to promote equitable access, appropriate services, and systemic change.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Model for Comprehensive and Integrated School Psychological Services (2020).

terms.definition: A derived test score indicating the average age of students who earned the same raw score; easily misinterpreted and generally less informative than standard scores.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A line on a progress monitoring graph connecting the student's baseline score to their goal score; used to evaluate whether the rate of improvement is sufficient to reach the goal.
terms.citation: CBM progress monitoring; Deno, S. L. (1985), 'Curriculum-based measurement: The emerging alternative,' Exceptional Children, 52(3), 219–232. National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research.

terms.definition: The legally required yearly IEP team meeting to review a student's progress, revise goals, and update services; mandated under IDEA.
Any stimulus, event, or condition occurring immediately before a behavior that may trigger or set the occasion for that behavior; the 'A' in the three-term ABC contingency.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Environmental or contextual factors present before a behavior occurs; identifying and modifying antecedents is often the most efficient first step in behavioral intervention.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: An emotional state involving excessive worry, apprehension, and physiological arousal; when persistent and impairing, may qualify as an anxiety disorder and can significantly interfere with learning.
A DSM-5 category of clinical disorders (e.g., Generalized Anxiety, Social Anxiety, Separation Anxiety) in which anxiety symptoms are excessive, persistent, and significantly impair daily functioning.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: See ABA; a science applying learning principles—especially reinforcement—to systematically analyze and improve socially significant behavior in real-world settings.
terms.citation: Baer, D. M., Wolf, M. M., & Risley, T. R. (1968), 'Some current dimensions of applied behavior analysis,' Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 1(1), 91–97; Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020), Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.).

terms.definition: Autism Spectrum Disorder; a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by deficits in social communication/interaction and restricted, repetitive behaviors; severity and support needs vary widely.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); IDEA special education category 'autism,' 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(1).

terms.definition: A child's or adolescent's agreement to participate in an evaluation or intervention; ethically required alongside parental consent for minors, though not legally binding independent of parental consent.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: The emotional bond between a child and primary caregiver; secure attachment supports healthy social-emotional development, while insecure patterns are linked to later social, emotional, and academic difficulties.
terms.citation: Bowlby, J. (1969). Attachment and Loss, Vol. 1. Basic Books; Ainsworth, M. D. S., et al. (1978). Patterns of Attachment.

terms.definition: The inattentive dimension of ADHD, characterized by difficulty sustaining attention, organizing tasks, and following through; may present without hyperactivity in some individuals.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: The brain's ability to interpret and use acoustic information; auditory processing disorder (APD) involves difficulty processing spoken language despite normal hearing acuity.
Performance-based tasks requiring students to apply knowledge in meaningful, real-world contexts; contrasted with traditional multiple-choice testing and valued for ecological validity.
A range of neurodevelopmental conditions defined by social communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors; see autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); IDEA special education category 'autism,' 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(1).

terms.definition: A DSM-5 neurodevelopmental disorder requiring persistent deficits in social communication/interaction across multiple contexts and restricted, repetitive behaviors; diagnosed based on severity of support needs.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); IDEA special education category 'autism,' 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(1).

terms.definition: Developmental, medical, educational, and family history gathered from records and interviews as part of a comprehensive evaluation; essential for contextualizing and interpreting assessment results.

Behavior Assessment System for Children; a widely used multi-informant rating scale measuring adaptive and problem behaviors (e.g., anxiety, aggression, leadership) across home, school, and clinical settings.
terms.citation: Reynolds, C. R., & Kamphaus, R. W., Behavior Assessment System for Children (BASC-3, 2015). Pearson.

terms.definition: The prevalence of a condition in a given population; a low base rate increases the likelihood of false positives even with a highly sensitive screening tool.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Any observable and measurable action of an organism; must be defined operationally (in specific, observable terms) for meaningful behavioral assessment and intervention planning.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: A standardized questionnaire completed by parents, teachers, or students to measure the frequency and severity of behavioral, emotional, and adaptive functioning symptoms.

Bergan's structured consultation model using operationally defined problems, data collection, and reinforcement-based plans; organized into problem identification, problem analysis, plan implementation, and plan evaluation phases.
terms.citation: Bergan, J. R., & Kratochwill, T. R. (1990). Behavioral Consultation and Therapy. Plenum Press.

terms.definition: A written agreement specifying target behaviors, performance criteria, and contingent reinforcers or consequences; involves the student and promotes shared accountability.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: A psychological school of thought holding that behavior is shaped by environmental contingencies (classical and operant conditioning); emphasizes observable, measurable behavior over internal mental events.
terms.citation: Watson, J. B. (1913), 'Psychology as the behaviorist views it,' Psychological Review, 20(2), 158–177; Skinner, B. F. (1953), Science and Human Behavior.

terms.definition: A performance standard at a specific point in time (e.g., end of first grade oral reading fluency of 60 wpm) indicating whether a student is on track to meet year-end goals.
terms.citation: National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research. CBM benchmarking (Deno, 1985).

terms.definition: The ability to use two languages with varying degrees of proficiency; in school psychology, refers to students who use two languages and require culturally and linguistically appropriate assessment.
A psychoeducational evaluation conducted in both the student's primary language and English to distinguish between a language difference and a true disability.
terms.citation: Cummins, J. (1984). Bilingualism and Special Education: Issues in Assessment and Pedagogy. Multilingual Matters.

terms.definition: Behavior Intervention Plan; a formal, written plan derived from an FBA that specifies proactive strategies, replacement behaviors, and consequence strategies to address challenging behavior.
terms.citation: IDEA discipline provisions, 34 C.F.R. § 300.530(f); see also positive behavior support literature (Center on PBIS).

terms.definition: A hierarchical framework of cognitive learning objectives ranging from lower-order (remembering, understanding, applying) to higher-order (analyzing, evaluating, creating); used in instruction and assessment design.
terms.citation: Bloom, B. S. (Ed.) (1956). Taxonomy of Educational Objectives: Handbook I. Longmans; revised by Anderson, L. W., & Krathwohl, D. R. (2001).

terms.definition: Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function; a rating scale measuring observable behaviors associated with executive function (working memory, inhibition, flexibility) in home and school settings.
terms.citation: Gioia, G. A., Isquith, P. K., Guy, S. C., & Kenworthy, L., Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF-2, 2015). PAR (Psychological Assessment Resources).

terms.definition: A short-term, structured, evidence-based intervention (often 1–5 sessions) targeting a specific concern; well-suited for school settings where time and access are limited.
Urie Bronfenbrenner; developmental psychologist who proposed the Ecological Systems Theory describing how nested environmental systems (microsystem through chronosystem) shape development.
terms.citation: Bronfenbrenner, U. (1979). The Ecology of Human Development. Harvard University Press.

terms.definition: Schoolwide programs and strategies aimed at reducing peer victimization, including direct, relational, and cyberbullying; effective programs involve multi-component approaches and school climate improvement.
terms.citation: Olweus, D. (1993). Bullying at School: What We Know and What We Can Do. Blackwell; Olweus Bullying Prevention Program.

terms.definition: Gerald Caplan; psychiatrist who developed the mental health consultation model focusing on consultee-centered consultation, in which the goal is building the consultee's own capacity to address future similar cases.
terms.citation: Caplan, G. (1970). The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation. Basic Books.

terms.definition: Curriculum-Based Measurement; brief, standardized, repeated academic probes (e.g., oral reading fluency) used for universal screening, progress monitoring, and data-based decision making within MTSS.
terms.citation: Deno, S. L. (1985), 'Curriculum-based measurement: The emerging alternative,' Exceptional Children, 52(3), 219–232.

terms.definition: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy; a structured, evidence-based therapeutic approach targeting maladaptive thoughts and behaviors; highly effective for anxiety, depression, and other internalizing disorders in youth.
terms.citation: Beck, A. T., Rush, A. J., Shaw, B. F., & Emery, G. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression. Guilford Press.

terms.definition: Occurs when a test is too easy for a student, producing scores clustered at the top of the scale and limiting the ability to differentiate among high performers.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A behavioral technique for teaching complex sequences of behavior by reinforcing successive links in a chain; can be taught forward (first step first) or backward (last step first).
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Pavlov's model in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it alone elicits a conditioned response; explains acquisition of anxiety and phobias.
terms.citation: Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned Reflexes (G. V. Anrep, Trans.). Oxford University Press.

terms.definition: Culturally and Linguistically Diverse; refers to students whose cultural background or primary language differs from the dominant school culture; requires culturally responsive and unbiased assessment practices.
In Caplan's model, consultation focused on the needs of the identified client (the student) rather than on developing the consultee's professional capacities.
terms.citation: Caplan, G. (1970). The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation. Basic Books.

terms.definition: General intellectual capacity including reasoning, memory, processing speed, and language; assessed with standardized cognitive batteries (e.g., WISC-V, WJ-IV); informs eligibility and instructional planning.

Evaluation of intellectual and cognitive functioning using standardized instruments; used for eligibility determinations, diagnosis, and to identify cognitive strengths and weaknesses for intervention.
The progression of thinking, reasoning, language, and problem-solving abilities; Piaget described four stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational.
terms.citation: Piaget's theory of cognitive development; Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: See CBT; a structured therapy integrating cognitive restructuring and behavioral strategies to treat internalizing and externalizing disorders.
terms.citation: Beck, A. T., Rush, A. J., Shaw, B. F., & Emery, G. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression. Guilford Press.

terms.definition: A standardized measure of effect size representing the difference between two means in standard deviation units; d = 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large; helps evaluate practical significance.
terms.citation: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

terms.definition: A consultation model in which consultant and consultee share expertise and responsibility as equals; contrasted with the expert model where the consultant directs solutions.
A structured, shared decision-making process in which all stakeholders (psychologist, teacher, parent) jointly define problems, analyze causes, and select interventions.
External organizations (mental health centers, child protective services, hospitals, nonprofits) that provide services to students and families beyond what schools can offer.
Programs, organizations, and services in the local community available to support student and family wellbeing; school psychologists connect families to appropriate resources.
The co-occurrence of two or more diagnoses or conditions in the same individual (e.g., ADHD and anxiety); common in school-age populations and typically complicates intervention planning.
Piaget's third cognitive stage (ages 7–11) in which children develop logical thinking about concrete objects and events but cannot yet reason abstractly or systematically.
terms.citation: Piaget's theory of cognitive development; Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: A DSM-5 diagnosis involving a persistent pattern of violating others' rights or major social norms (aggression, property destruction, deceitfulness, theft); often precedes adult antisocial behavior.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: A range of values (usually 95%) that likely contains the student's true score; preferred over reporting a single point score because it communicates measurement uncertainty.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: The ethical and legal obligation to protect student information from unauthorized disclosure; bounded by mandatory reporting obligations, safety concerns, and FERPA regulations.
terms.citation: NASP Principles for Professional Ethics (2020); FERPA, 20 U.S.C. § 1232g.

terms.definition: An extraneous variable related to both the independent and dependent variable that may account for an observed effect, undermining causal conclusions.
See confound; a variable that co-varies with the treatment condition and could explain observed outcomes, threatening a study's internal validity.
Involving both home and school systems simultaneously; as in conjoint behavioral consultation, which engages parents and teachers as collaborative partners in problem-solving.
terms.citation: Sheridan, S. M., & Kratochwill, T. R. (2008). Conjoint Behavioral Consultation (2nd ed.). Springer.

terms.definition: Susan Sheridan's consultation model engaging parents and teachers as co-equal partners across home and school settings; strengthens generalization and home-school communication.
terms.citation: Sheridan, S. M., & Kratochwill, T. R. (2008). Conjoint Behavioral Consultation: Promoting Family-School Connections and Interventions (2nd ed.). Springer.

terms.definition: A widely used rating scale for assessing ADHD symptoms and related problems; available in parent, teacher, and self-report versions and normed for children and adolescents.
terms.citation: Conners, C. K., Conners (3rd ed.) / Conners CBRS. Multi-Health Systems (MHS).

terms.definition: Any stimulus or event occurring immediately after a behavior that influences its future likelihood; reinforcing consequences increase behavior, punishing consequences decrease it.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: The degree to which a test measures the theoretical construct it purports to measure (e.g., whether an 'intelligence' test actually measures intelligence vs. test-taking familiarity).
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A learning theory proposing that learners actively construct knowledge through experience and reflection; associated with Piaget and Vygotsky; informs discovery-based instructional approaches.
terms.citation: Associated with Piaget (1952) and Vygotsky (1978); see also Bruner, J. S. (1966).

terms.definition: In a consultation relationship, the professional (often the school psychologist) who provides expertise and support to help the consultee address a client's needs.
A structured problem-solving interaction typically organized into four phases: problem identification, problem analysis, plan implementation, and plan evaluation.
terms.citation: Bergan, J. R., & Kratochwill, T. R. (1990). Behavioral Consultation and Therapy. Plenum Press.

terms.definition: In a consultation relationship, the professional (teacher, parent, or administrator) who works directly with the client (student) and seeks support from the consultant.
A focus in consultation on improving the consultee's professional skills, objectivity, or confidence rather than solving the presenting problem directly.
terms.citation: Caplan, G. (1970). The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation. Basic Books.

terms.definition: Caplan's model in which the primary goal is improving the consultee's professional functioning (knowledge, skill, confidence, objectivity) so they can serve future clients more effectively.
terms.citation: Caplan, G. (1970). The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation. Basic Books.

terms.definition: The extent to which test items adequately and representatively sample the full domain of the construct being assessed; typically established through expert review and systematic item development.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: In experimental research, the group not receiving the treatment (independent variable); compared with the experimental group to determine the causal effect of the intervention.
Specific, timely feedback provided when a student or consultee performs incorrectly; effective feedback identifies the error and redirects toward the correct response.
A statistical measure of the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables; ranges from -1.0 (perfect negative) to +1.0 (perfect positive); does not imply causation.
A research design examining relationships between variables without experimental manipulation; cannot establish causation but is useful for prediction and hypothesis generation.
Immediate, short-term psychological support for individuals in acute distress to restore safety and pre-crisis functioning; school psychologists often follow structured protocols (e.g., PREPaRE).
terms.citation: NASP PREPaRE model; Brock, S. E., et al. (2016). School Crisis Prevention and Intervention: The PREPaRE Model (2nd ed.). NASP.

terms.definition: An assessment approach comparing a student's performance to a fixed performance standard or mastery level rather than to the performance of other students.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A coefficient measuring internal consistency reliability, indicating how strongly test items correlate with each other; values above .70 are generally considered adequate.
terms.citation: Cronbach, L. J. (1951), 'Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests,' Psychometrika, 16(3), 297–334; see also Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Gc; accumulated verbal knowledge and language-based skills acquired through education and experience; tends to be stable or increase with age.
terms.citation: Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) theory of cognitive abilities; McGrew, K. S. (2009), Intelligence, 37(1), 1–10.

terms.definition: The ability to work effectively with people from diverse cultural backgrounds; requires self-awareness, knowledge of cultural differences, and adaptation of professional practices.
terms.citation: Sue, D. W., Arredondo, P., & McDavis, R. J. (1992), 'Multicultural counseling competencies and standards,' Journal of Counseling & Development; NASP Model for Comprehensive and Integrated School Psychological Services (2020).

terms.definition: Integrating respect for and knowledge of students' cultural backgrounds into professional practice; required for valid assessment and effective intervention with diverse populations.
terms.citation: Gay, G. (2018). Culturally Responsive Teaching: Theory, Research, and Practice (3rd ed.). Teachers College Press.

terms.definition: See CLD; students whose cultural and/or linguistic background differs from the dominant school culture; valid assessment requires eliminating language and cultural bias.
Approaches that honor and incorporate students' cultural backgrounds, values, and communication styles into instruction, assessment, and intervention to improve relevance and outcomes.
terms.citation: Gay, G. (2018). Culturally Responsive Teaching: Theory, Research, and Practice (3rd ed.). Teachers College Press.

terms.definition: See CBM; brief, standardized academic probes yielding repeated, comparable measures of a student's skill growth over time within the instructional curriculum.
terms.citation: Deno, S. L. (1985), 'Curriculum-based measurement: The emerging alternative,' Exceptional Children, 52(3), 219–232.

terms.definition: Bullying conducted through digital platforms (social media, texting, online games); can be especially harmful due to its pervasive reach and potential for large audiences.
terms.citation: Hinduja, S., & Patchin, J. W., Cyberbullying Research Center (cyberbullying.org).

terms.definition: Using systematically collected, objective data to guide instructional and intervention decisions rather than relying on intuition; a core principle of MTSS and school psychology practice.
terms.citation: National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research. NASP Model for Comprehensive and Integrated School Psychological Services (2020).

terms.definition: A pre-established criterion for making data-based decisions; for example, if a student's scores fall below the aim line for 3 consecutive probes, the intervention should be modified.
terms.citation: Data-based decision making in MTSS; National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research.

terms.definition: Applying phoneme-grapheme correspondence rules to identify unfamiliar printed words; a foundational reading skill frequently assessed in evaluations for reading disabilities.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: The outcome variable measured in an experiment to assess the effect of the independent variable; the 'result' or 'effect' side of a cause-and-effect relationship.
A mood condition characterized by persistent sadness, anhedonia, fatigue, and impaired daily functioning; one of the most common mental health concerns in school-age youth.
A DSM-5 category including Major Depressive Disorder and Persistent Depressive Disorder, defined by prolonged low mood, loss of interest, and significant functional impairment.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Statistical measures that organize and summarize data (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, frequency); describe characteristics of a sample without drawing inferences.
Information about a child's early development (prenatal/birth factors, developmental milestones, medical history) gathered as part of a comprehensive evaluation to contextualize current functioning.
A comprehensive evaluation used to identify the specific nature, severity, and causes of a student's difficulties; goes deeper than screening and guides targeted intervention planning.
The specific signs, symptoms, duration, and impairment thresholds listed in DSM-5 that must be met for a clinical diagnosis; ensure standardized, consistent identification.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Tailoring instruction to meet individual students' readiness, interests, and learning profiles by varying content, process, product, or environment within the same classroom.
terms.citation: Tomlinson, C. A. (2014). The Differentiated Classroom: Responding to the Needs of All Learners (2nd ed.). ASCD.

terms.definition: An explicit, structured teaching method characterized by clear modeling, high rates of academic engagement, guided practice with immediate feedback, and mastery-based progression; evidence-based for basic skills.
terms.citation: Engelmann, S., & Carnine, D. (1991). Theory of Instruction: Principles and Applications (rev. ed.). NIFDI Press.

terms.definition: The determination by a multidisciplinary team that a student meets IDEA criteria for a specific disability category, qualifying them for special education and related services.
The overrepresentation or underrepresentation of students from specific racial or ethnic groups in special education categories, gifted programs, or disciplinary actions.
terms.citation: IDEA disproportionality provisions, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.646–300.647; National Research Council, Donovan & Cross (Eds.) (2002), Minority Students in Special and Gifted Education.

terms.definition: The range of human differences (race, ethnicity, language, gender, ability, socioeconomic status, religion); school psychologists must demonstrate competence with diverse student populations.
Differential Reinforcement of Alternative Behavior; a behavioral procedure that reinforces a specific, acceptable alternative behavior to replace a problem behavior.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Differential Reinforcement of Incompatible Behavior; reinforcing a behavior that is physically impossible to perform simultaneously with the problem behavior.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Differential Reinforcement of Other Behavior; providing reinforcement after a specified interval during which the problem behavior did NOT occur; reduces problem behavior without selecting a replacement.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition; the American Psychiatric Association's classification system for mental disorders; used to diagnose conditions like ADHD, ASD, and mood disorders.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: A situation in which a school psychologist has both a professional role and another type of relationship (personal, financial, supervisory) with a student or family; ethically problematic.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: Formal IDEA dispute resolution procedures protecting parents' rights to challenge eligibility, placement, or services through an impartial hearing; a last resort after less formal options.
The ethical and legal obligation to take reasonable steps to protect identifiable potential victims from credible, serious threats; derived from the Tarasoff ruling.
terms.citation: Derived from Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California, 17 Cal. 3d 425 (1976).

terms.definition: An assessment approach using a test-teach-retest format to evaluate a student's responsiveness to instruction and learning potential, rather than measuring only current knowledge.
terms.citation: Lidz, C. S. (1987). Dynamic Assessment: An Interactional Approach to Evaluating Learning Potential. Guilford Press; Feuerstein, R., et al.

terms.definition: A specific learning disability affecting the acquisition of mathematical skills (number sense, arithmetic facts, math reasoning); analogous to dyslexia in reading.
terms.citation: DSM-5 specific learning disorder with impairment in mathematics (APA, 2013); IDEA SLD category, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10).

terms.definition: A specific learning disability affecting written expression, including handwriting, spelling, and composition; not simply poor penmanship but a deficit in the writing process itself.
terms.citation: DSM-5 specific learning disorder with impairment in written expression (APA, 2013); IDEA SLD category, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10).

terms.definition: A specific learning disability characterized by difficulties with accurate and/or fluent word recognition, poor decoding, and poor spelling; neurobiological in origin and responsive to explicit reading instruction.
terms.citation: International Dyslexia Association (IDA) definition (2002); IDEA SLD category, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10).

terms.definition: Evidence-Based Practice; professional decision-making integrating the best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and client characteristics; school psychologists are expected to use EBPs.
terms.citation: American Psychological Association (2006), 'Evidence-based practice in psychology,' American Psychologist, 61(4), 271–285; What Works Clearinghouse (IES).

terms.definition: Evaluation of the environments in which a student functions (classroom, home, peer group) to identify contextual factors contributing to academic or behavioral difficulties.

Emotional Disturbance; an IDEA special education eligibility category for students with serious emotional/behavioral difficulties that adversely affect educational performance and are not due to other conditions.
Documents and data about a student maintained by a school; protected under FERPA with parents having rights to access, review, and request amendments.
terms.citation: FERPA, 20 U.S.C. § 1232g; 34 C.F.R. Part 99; IDEA confidentiality provisions, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.611–300.625.

terms.definition: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of an intervention's impact; used alongside statistical significance to evaluate practical importance (e.g., Cohen's d, odds ratio).
terms.citation: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

terms.definition: English Learner; a student who is developing English proficiency and whose home language is other than English; see also English Language Learner (ELL).
The multidisciplinary team's data-based decision about whether a student meets IDEA criteria for a specific disability category and qualifies for special education.
English Language Learner; a student not yet proficient in English whose primary language is other than English; requires culturally and linguistically appropriate instruction and assessment.
See ED; an IDEA eligibility category covering students with significant, chronic emotional or behavioral problems that impair educational performance.

Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District (2017); Supreme Court ruling clarifying that IDEA requires IEPs to be sufficiently ambitious—students must have a realistic chance to make meaningful progress.
terms.citation: Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District RE-1, 580 U.S. 386 (2017).

terms.definition: Obstacles preventing families from participating in school activities or educational decision-making; may include language differences, work demands, distrust, or prior negative experiences with schools.
A student whose primary language is other than English and who is developing English proficiency; instruction and assessment must account for language development stage.
See ELL; a student developing English proficiency whose home language is other than English; used interchangeably with English Language Learner.
Fair treatment, access, opportunity, and advancement for all students; requires actively addressing systemic barriers and not just treating everyone identically.
Erik Erikson; developmental psychologist known for his eight-stage psychosocial theory (e.g., trust vs. mistrust, industry vs. inferiority, identity vs. role confusion).
terms.citation: Erikson, E. H. (1950). Childhood and Society. Norton.

terms.definition: A systematic process for resolving ethical dilemmas by applying ethical principles, professional standards, relevant laws, and consideration of all stakeholders' interests.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: An intervention supported by rigorous peer-reviewed research demonstrating effectiveness for a specific population and problem; preferred in all MTSS tiers.
terms.citation: What Works Clearinghouse (WWC), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.

terms.definition: Integration of the best available research, clinical expertise, and client preferences/characteristics when making professional decisions; the gold standard for school psychology practice.
terms.citation: American Psychological Association (2006), 'Evidence-based practice in psychology,' American Psychologist, 61(4), 271–285; What Works Clearinghouse (IES).

terms.definition: Disciplinary practices (suspension, expulsion) that remove students from educational settings; associated with disproportionality, reduced academic engagement, and negative long-term outcomes.
terms.citation: IDEA discipline procedures, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.530–300.536.

terms.definition: A set of higher-order cognitive processes (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, planning) that regulate goal-directed behavior; frequently impaired in ADHD and LD.
terms.citation: Diamond, A. (2013), 'Executive functions,' Annual Review of Psychology, 64, 135–168.

terms.definition: A research design using random assignment to conditions, enabling causal conclusions about the effect of an independent variable; the strongest design for establishing effectiveness.
The group in an experiment that receives the independent variable (treatment); compared to the control group to determine the intervention's effect.
Conscious, deliberate attitudes or stereotypes about a social group; contrasted with implicit bias, which operates below awareness; both can lead to inequitable decisions.
A systematic, structured teaching approach involving clear modeling, adequate guided practice with feedback, and independent practice; highly effective for basic academic skills.
terms.citation: Archer, A. L., & Hughes, C. A. (2011). Explicit Instruction: Effective and Efficient Teaching. Guilford Press.

terms.definition: The most severe exclusionary discipline, removing a student from school for an extended period; students with disabilities are entitled to procedural protections under IDEA.
terms.citation: IDEA discipline procedures, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.530–300.536.

terms.definition: An accommodation providing additional time to complete assessments or assignments; appropriate for many students with disabilities including learning disabilities and ADHD.
The degree to which research findings can be generalized to other populations, settings, and conditions beyond those studied.
Behavioral and emotional problems directed outward (aggression, defiance, conduct problems, hyperactivity); contrasted with internalizing problems.
terms.citation: Achenbach, T. M. (1991). Manual for the Child Behavior Checklist/4-18. University of Vermont.

terms.definition: The removal of reinforcement for a previously reinforced behavior, resulting in a gradual decrease in that behavior; may initially cause a temporary extinction burst.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: A screening result indicating the condition is absent when it is actually present; a missed case; particularly harmful when early identification is critical.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A screening result indicating the condition is present when it is actually absent; leads to unnecessary referrals or over-identification; especially costly with low base rates.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Active, meaningful family participation in a child's education across school and home settings; consistently linked to improved academic and social-emotional outcomes.
A theoretical framework viewing the family as an interconnected system where changes in any member affect all others; guides family-centered assessment and intervention.
terms.citation: Bowen, M. (1978). Family Therapy in Clinical Practice. Jason Aronson; Minuchin, S. (1974). Families and Family Therapy.

terms.definition: Free Appropriate Public Education; IDEA's core guarantee that students with disabilities receive special education and related services at no cost to parents, tailored to their unique needs.
Functional Behavioral Assessment; a process identifying the function (purpose) of a behavior by analyzing antecedents, behaviors, and consequences to develop a function-based BIP.
terms.citation: Referenced in IDEA discipline provisions, 34 C.F.R. § 300.530(d)–(f); methodology: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act; federal law granting parents (and students 18+) rights to access educational records and restricting disclosure without consent.
terms.citation: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), 20 U.S.C. § 1232g; 34 C.F.R. Part 99.

terms.definition: The degree to which an intervention is implemented as designed; low fidelity makes it impossible to determine whether poor outcomes are due to the intervention or its implementation.
See treatment integrity; the consistency and completeness with which an intervention is delivered according to its protocol; critical for valid outcome interpretation.
A stage of the instructional hierarchy between acquisition and generalization, characterized by performing a skill both accurately and at an adequate rate.
terms.citation: Instructional hierarchy; Haring, N. G., Lovitt, T. C., Eaton, M. D., & Hansen, C. L. (1978). The Fourth R: Research in the Classroom. Merrill.

terms.definition: Gf; the capacity to solve novel problems and think logically independent of previously acquired knowledge; assessed by nonverbal reasoning and inductive/deductive reasoning tasks.
terms.citation: Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) theory of cognitive abilities; McGrew, K. S. (2009), Intelligence, 37(1), 1–10.

terms.definition: Piaget's fourth and final cognitive stage (emerging around age 12), characterized by abstract reasoning, hypothetical-deductive thinking, and systematic problem-solving.
terms.citation: Piaget's theory of cognitive development; Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: Ongoing assessment during instruction used to monitor learning, provide feedback, and adjust teaching; examples include CBM probes, exit tickets, and teacher observation.
terms.citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998), 'Assessment and classroom learning,' Assessment in Education, 5(1), 7–74.

terms.definition: See FAPE; the IDEA entitlement ensuring students with disabilities receive special education at public expense that is appropriate for their individual needs.
See FBA; a comprehensive, systematic process identifying why a behavior occurs by examining the antecedent-behavior-consequence sequence to guide intervention.
terms.citation: Referenced in IDEA discipline provisions, 34 C.F.R. § 300.530(d)–(f); methodology: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Transfer of a learned skill to different people, settings, or materials beyond the original training context; often the most difficult stage of the instructional hierarchy to achieve.
terms.citation: Stokes, T. F., & Baer, D. M. (1977), 'An implicit technology of generalization,' Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 10(2), 349–367; instructional hierarchy (Haring et al., 1978).

terms.definition: A derived score indicating the grade level of students who on average earned the same raw score; often misinterpreted and generally less preferred than standard scores.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Requiring a student to repeat a grade level; research generally does not support retention as an effective long-term academic intervention and may harm social-emotional outcomes.
terms.citation: Jimerson, S. R. (2001), 'Meta-analysis of grade retention research: Implications for practice,' School Psychology Review, 30(3), 420–437.

terms.definition: A visual tool (mind map, concept map, Venn diagram) used to organize and display knowledge and relationships between concepts; improves comprehension and retention.
The natural emotional response to loss (death, divorce, separation); school psychologists support bereaved students through counseling, psychoeducation, and referral when needed.
A therapeutic format in which a small number of students with similar concerns meet with a counselor; evidence-based for social skills, grief, anxiety, and coping.
The proportion of variance in a trait within a population attributable to genetic differences; does not mean the trait is fixed or that environment is unimportant.
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act; federal law protecting the privacy of health information held by healthcare providers; applies to school-based mental health providers.
terms.citation: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, Pub. L. No. 104-191; HIPAA Privacy Rule, 45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164.

terms.definition: An internal validity threat where external events occurring simultaneously with an intervention (not the intervention itself) could explain changes in the dependent variable.
Partnership between families and school personnel to support student learning and wellbeing; associated with improved academic and social-emotional outcomes.
Excessive, persistent motor activity (fidgeting, leaving seat, running/climbing inappropriately); one of the two core ADHD symptom dimensions; must be impairing across settings.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Intellectual Disability; a disability characterized by significant limitations in both intellectual functioning (IQ ≤ ~70) and adaptive behavior, originating before age 18.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(6); American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) (2021), Intellectual Disability: Definition, Classification, and Systems of Supports (12th ed.).

terms.definition: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act; the federal law mandating free appropriate public education for eligible students with disabilities and governing special education services.
terms.citation: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), 20 U.S.C. § 1400 et seq.; 34 C.F.R. Part 300.

terms.definition: Individualized Education Program; a legally required written document for each student with a disability specifying present levels, annual goals, special education services, and placement.
The required meeting of the IEP team to develop, review, or revise a student's IEP; parents have the right to participate and must receive prior written notice.
The multidisciplinary group legally required to develop and monitor the IEP; must include parents, a general education teacher, a special education teacher, and an LEA representative.
See fidelity; the degree to which a program or intervention is delivered as designed; necessary for valid interpretation of outcome data.
Unconscious attitudes or stereotypes about social groups that affect judgments and behavior below conscious awareness; contributes to disproportionality in special education referrals.
terms.citation: Greenwald, A. G., & Banaji, M. R. (1995), 'Implicit social cognition: Attitudes, self-esteem, and stereotypes,' Psychological Review, 102(1), 4–27.

terms.definition: Acting without adequate forethought or self-control; a core dimension of ADHD that impairs social relationships, academic performance, and safety.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Difficulty sustaining focus, following directions, and organizing tasks; one of the two core ADHD symptom dimensions; may present without prominent hyperactivity.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Educating students with disabilities alongside non-disabled peers in general education settings with appropriate supports; aligned with IDEA's least restrictive environment mandate.
terms.citation: Rooted in IDEA's least restrictive environment requirement, 20 U.S.C. § 1412(a)(5); 34 C.F.R. § 300.114.

terms.definition: The variable deliberately manipulated by the researcher to test its effect on the dependent variable; the 'cause' in a cause-and-effect relationship.
One-on-one therapeutic support between a counselor and student to address emotional, behavioral, or academic concerns; may be preventive, responsive, or crisis-oriented.
See IEP; the cornerstone legal document for special education services, individualized for each eligible student with a disability.
See IDEA; the federal special education law guaranteeing FAPE and procedural safeguards for students with disabilities.
terms.citation: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), 20 U.S.C. § 1400 et seq.; 34 C.F.R. Part 300.

terms.definition: Voluntary, knowledgeable agreement to participate in an evaluation or service following full disclosure of procedures, risks, benefits, and the right to withdraw.
terms.citation: IDEA definition of consent, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.9, 300.300; see also NASP Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: The ability to suppress prepotent but irrelevant responses and distracting stimuli; a core executive function that is often impaired in ADHD and associated disorders.
terms.citation: Diamond, A. (2013), 'Executive functions,' Annual Review of Psychology, 64, 135–168.

terms.definition: A disability with onset before age 18 characterized by significant limitations in intellectual functioning (IQ ≤ ~70) and adaptive behavior across conceptual, social, and practical domains.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(6); American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) (2021), Intellectual Disability: Definition, Classification, and Systems of Supports (12th ed.).

terms.definition: Tier 3 support; the most individualized, data-driven instruction for students who do not respond adequately to Tier 1 or Tier 2 interventions; may lead to special education referral.
terms.citation: MTSS Tier 3; National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research.

terms.definition: Coordination among multiple service systems (schools, mental health, child welfare, juvenile justice) to provide comprehensive, wraparound services to students with complex needs.
A reliability estimate measuring how strongly all items on a test correlate with each other, indicating they assess the same underlying construct; typically measured with Cronbach's alpha.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: The degree to which an experimental study establishes a causal relationship between the independent and dependent variable; threatened by confounds, history, maturation, and selection bias.
Behavioral and emotional problems directed inward (anxiety, depression, somatic complaints, withdrawal); contrasted with externalizing problems.
terms.citation: Achenbach, T. M. (1991). Manual for the Child Behavior Checklist/4-18. University of Vermont.

terms.definition: The degree to which two or more independent raters assign identical scores or classifications; especially critical for behavioral observation and scoring subjective responses.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A structured or unstructured method of gathering information from informants (parents, teachers, students); one component of the RIOT framework and essential for ecological assessment.
A standardized intelligence test measuring overall cognitive ability; most use mean = 100, SD = 15; examples include WISC-V and Stanford-Binet 5.
The process by which children develop the ability to understand and produce language; second language acquisition follows predictable developmental stages.
Impaired ability to understand (receptive) or use (expressive) language for communication; can affect listening, speaking, reading, writing, and social communication.
The degree to which an individual has mastered a language's components (listening, speaking, reading, writing); must be assessed to conduct valid evaluations of ELL students.
terms.citation: Cummins, J. (1984). Bilingualism and Special Education: Issues in Assessment and Pedagogy. Multilingual Matters (BICS/CALP distinction).

terms.definition: A 1979 federal ruling finding that IQ tests were culturally biased against African American students; restricted IQ test use for Black students' special education placement in California.
terms.citation: Larry P. v. Riles, 793 F.2d 969 (9th Cir. 1984), aff'g 495 F. Supp. 926 (N.D. Cal. 1979).

terms.definition: See specific learning disability (SLD); an IDEA category involving unexpected academic difficulty in one or more areas despite adequate intelligence and appropriate instruction.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10); SLD identification procedures, §§ 300.307–300.311.

terms.definition: See LRE; the IDEA requirement that students with disabilities be educated alongside non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate.
An ongoing commitment to professional growth, skill development, and staying current with research throughout one's career; an ethical obligation under NASP standards.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: Least Restrictive Environment; the IDEA principle that students with disabilities must be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate given their needs.
The legal obligation of school professionals to report known or suspected child abuse or neglect to designated authorities; overrides confidentiality obligations.
terms.citation: Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act (CAPTA), 42 U.S.C. § 5101 et seq.; specific mandated-reporter duties are defined by state statute.

terms.definition: A required IDEA review when a student with a disability faces a disciplinary change of placement; determines whether the behavior was caused by or related to the disability or its implementation.
The arithmetic average of a set of scores; the most commonly used measure of central tendency; sensitive to extreme outliers.
The middle value when scores are rank-ordered; preferred over the mean when data are skewed or include outliers.
An IDEA dispute resolution option in which a neutral third party helps parents and school reach voluntary agreement; less adversarial than due process hearings.
A state of psychological wellbeing that enables individuals to cope with life's stresses, work productively, and contribute to community; a primary focus area for school psychologists.
Caplan's model addressing the mental health needs of clients through the consultee; includes consultee-centered and client-centered forms, and focuses on building consultee capacity.
terms.citation: Caplan, G. (1970). The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation. Basic Books.

terms.definition: A statistical method combining results from multiple independent studies to produce a single overall estimate of an intervention's effect; provides stronger evidence than any individual study.
terms.citation: Borenstein, M., Hedges, L. V., Higgins, J. P. T., & Rothstein, H. R. (2009). Introduction to Meta-Analysis. Wiley.

terms.definition: Awareness and regulation of one's own thinking and learning processes, including planning, monitoring comprehension, and evaluating strategy effectiveness; strongly linked to academic success.
terms.citation: Flavell, J. H. (1979), 'Metacognition and cognitive monitoring,' American Psychologist, 34(10), 906–911.

terms.definition: Motivational Interviewing; a collaborative, person-centered counseling approach that elicits behavior change by exploring and resolving ambivalence through reflective listening and open-ended questions.
terms.citation: Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2013). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

terms.definition: A 1972 federal case establishing that all children with disabilities are entitled to a free public education regardless of the severity of disability or cost to the school district.
terms.citation: Mills v. Board of Education of District of Columbia, 348 F. Supp. 866 (D.D.C. 1972).

terms.definition: A memory strategy using acronyms, rhymes, imagery, or elaboration to encode and retrieve information more effectively; evidence-based for students with learning and memory difficulties.
The most frequently occurring value in a dataset; can be more appropriate than mean or median for nominal data or multimodal distributions.
Changes to the curriculum content, expected learning outcomes, or assessment standards (not just delivery); they alter what is expected of the student, unlike accommodations.
A DSM-5 category of disorders characterized by persistent disturbances in emotional tone, including depressive disorders and bipolar and related disorders.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: The progression of understanding right, wrong, and ethical reasoning; Kohlberg described three levels: preconventional, conventional, and postconventional reasoning.
terms.citation: Kohlberg, L. (1984). The Psychology of Moral Development. Harper & Row.

terms.definition: See MI; a client-centered, directive method using reflective listening, affirmation, and open-ended questions to strengthen an individual's intrinsic motivation for change.
terms.citation: Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2013). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

terms.definition: Multi-Tiered System of Supports; a prevention-oriented framework delivering increasingly intensive levels of instruction and support (Tier 1, 2, 3) based on ongoing student data.
terms.citation: Center on Multi-Tiered System of Supports (mtss4success.org), American Institutes for Research, funded by U.S. Dept. of Education OSEP.

terms.definition: Gathering assessment data from multiple sources (parents, teachers, student) across settings; provides a more comprehensive and valid picture than any single informant.
Using multiple types of assessment tools (interviews, observations, tests, records review) to gather evaluation data; essential for valid, comprehensive assessment (aligns with RIOT).
See MTSS; a framework aligning resources across all students using universal screening, evidence-based instruction, and data-based decision making.
terms.citation: Center on Multi-Tiered System of Supports (mtss4success.org), American Institutes for Research, funded by U.S. Dept. of Education OSEP.

terms.definition: Pertaining to the coexistence of multiple cultural groups; multicultural competence requires self-awareness, cultural knowledge, and adaptation of practice to diverse populations.
A group of professionals from different disciplines (psychology, special education, speech, medicine) who collaborate to evaluate a student and make eligibility decisions.
Collecting assessment information from various informants and settings; required for valid special education evaluations under IDEA and for comprehensive FBAs.
The ethical guidelines and professional standards set by the National Association of School Psychologists; govern all aspects of school psychology practice.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: NASP's official ethical code organized around four themes: Responsibility to Students, Responsibility to Schools and Communities, Professional Competency, and Responsibility to the Profession.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: A systematic process identifying the gap between current and desired states in knowledge, skills, or services; informs program planning and resource allocation.
The removal of an aversive stimulus following a behavior, increasing the future probability of that behavior; negative reinforcement is not punishment—it increases behavior.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Pertaining to brain development and its effects on cognitive, behavioral, and emotional functioning; neurodevelopmental disorders include ADHD, ASD, SLD, and intellectual disability.
Describing an equal-partner relationship between consultant and consultee, where both contribute unique expertise; contrasted with expert-driven consultation models.
An assessment approach comparing an individual's performance to a standardization sample; yields scores (standard scores, percentile ranks) indicating relative standing.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution in which most scores cluster near the mean with fewer at the extremes; the basis for interpreting standard scores on most cognitive tests.
A study skill involving recording key information during instruction or reading; can be explicitly taught and is associated with improved retention and academic performance.
Systematic, direct recording of a student's behavior in a natural setting; part of the RIOT framework and essential for ecological assessment and FBA.
Oppositional Defiant Disorder; a DSM-5 disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of irritable/angry mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, and/or vindictiveness toward authority figures.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Skinner's model of learning in which behavior is shaped by its consequences; reinforcement increases behavior and punishment decreases it; foundational to behavioral interventions.
terms.citation: Skinner, B. F. (1938). The Behavior of Organisms. Appleton-Century-Crofts.

terms.definition: See ODD; characterized by persistent noncompliance, defiance, and hostility directed at authority figures; often co-occurs with ADHD.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: Consultation focused on improving systems, policies, or organizational structures rather than addressing individual student or consultee concerns.

A disproportionately high percentage of students from a specific demographic group (often racial minorities) in special education or disciplinary categories relative to their share of the school population.
terms.citation: IDEA disproportionality provisions, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.646–300.647; National Research Council, Donovan & Cross (Eds.) (2002), Minority Students in Special and Gifted Education.

terms.definition: The probability of obtaining results as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true; a p < .05 threshold means results are unlikely due to chance, but does not indicate effect size.
Family participation in children's education at home and school; associated with improved academic achievement, motivation, and school attendance.
Legal rights guaranteed to parents under IDEA and FERPA, including rights to consent, access records, participate in IEP meetings, and pursue dispute resolution.
Structured programs teaching parents behavioral strategies (e.g., praise, consistent consequences, communication skills) to support their child's development and reduce challenging behavior.
Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports; a tiered, data-driven framework applying behavioral principles schoolwide to promote positive behavior and prevent problem behavior.
terms.citation: Center on Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (pbis.org), U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (OSEP). Referenced in IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.324(a)(2)(i).

terms.definition: A derived score indicating the percentage of the norm group that scored at or below a given raw score; a score at the 75th percentile means the student outperformed 75% of peers.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: The ability to hear, identify, and manipulate individual phonemes (smallest sound units) in spoken words; the most critical phonological awareness skill for reading acquisition.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: Instruction explicitly teaching the systematic relationships between letters (graphemes) and sounds (phonemes) to develop word decoding and spelling skills.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: The ability to recognize and manipulate sound structures of language at multiple levels (words, syllables, rhymes, phonemes); a strong predictor of reading success.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: Using sound-based information to process language; includes phonological awareness, phonological working memory (digit span), and rapid automatized naming.
terms.citation: Wagner, R. K., & Torgesen, J. K. (1987), 'The nature of phonological processing and its causal role in the acquisition of reading skills,' Psychological Bulletin, 101(2), 192–212.

terms.definition: Jean Piaget; Swiss developmental psychologist who proposed the four-stage theory of cognitive development: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational.
terms.citation: Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: A therapeutic approach using play as the primary medium for communication with children; helps children express feelings, process trauma, and develop adaptive coping strategies.
terms.citation: Axline, V. M. (1947). Play Therapy. Houghton Mifflin; Landreth, G. L. (2012). Play Therapy: The Art of the Relationship (3rd ed.).

terms.definition: Professional Learning Community; a collaborative team of educators who regularly share data, goals, and strategies to improve student learning outcomes.
A purposeful collection of student work samples over time used to demonstrate growth, effort, and achievement; a form of authentic assessment emphasizing process as well as product.
An evidence-based, function-based approach using proactive, positive strategies and environmental modifications to promote appropriate behavior and prevent problem behavior.
terms.citation: Center on Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (pbis.org), U.S. Dept. of Education OSEP; Sugai, G., & Horner, R. H. (2009).

terms.definition: Providing a desired stimulus following a behavior to increase the future probability of that behavior; the most consistently effective strategy for building new behaviors.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Psychological symptoms following exposure to a traumatic event, including intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, and negative changes in cognition/mood; see PTSD.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).

terms.definition: The real-world meaningfulness of an effect, assessed by effect size rather than p-value; a statistically significant result can have minimal practical importance.
The social use of language in context, including turn-taking, inferencing, adjusting communication style, and understanding figurative language; impaired in ASD and social communication disorder.
Interventions and problem-solving efforts implemented before formally referring a student for a special education evaluation; ensures learning difficulties aren't due to lack of instruction.
terms.citation: IDEA child find, 34 C.F.R. § 300.111; see also RTI/SLD identification, §§ 300.307–300.311.

terms.definition: A type of criterion validity in which test scores correlate with a future criterion outcome (e.g., a kindergarten screening predicting first-grade reading achievement).
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Piaget's second cognitive stage (ages 2–7), characterized by symbolic thinking and language use but limited by egocentrism, centration, and irreversibility.
terms.citation: Piaget's theory of cognitive development; Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: A written document schools must send to parents before proposing or refusing any change in identification, evaluation, educational placement, or provision of FAPE.
A brief, standardized sample used in CBM to quickly measure a student's academic skill (e.g., a 1-minute oral reading fluency passage); administered repeatedly to track growth.
terms.citation: Curriculum-based measurement; Deno, S. L. (1985), 'Curriculum-based measurement: The emerging alternative,' Exceptional Children, 52(3), 219–232.

terms.definition: The second phase of the consultation process; identifying why the problem is occurring by analyzing data, generating hypotheses about contributing factors, and selecting an intervention.
terms.citation: Bergan, J. R., & Kratochwill, T. R. (1990). Behavioral Consultation and Therapy. Plenum Press.

terms.definition: The first phase of the consultation process; operationally defining the problem, gathering baseline data, and specifying a measurable goal.
terms.citation: Bergan, J. R., & Kratochwill, T. R. (1990). Behavioral Consultation and Therapy. Plenum Press.

terms.definition: A systematic, data-based framework for identifying student needs, analyzing causes, selecting and implementing interventions, and evaluating outcomes; the foundation of MTSS.
terms.citation: Data-based problem-solving model; NASP Model for Comprehensive and Integrated School Psychological Services (2020); Bergan & Kratochwill (1990).

terms.definition: Legal protections under IDEA ensuring parents' rights throughout the special education process, including notification, consent, records access, and dispute resolution options.
The rate at which a person can perform simple, repetitive cognitive tasks; assessed by subtests like Coding and Symbol Search; slower processing often co-occurs with ADHD and LD.
terms.citation: Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) theory of cognitive abilities; McGrew, K. S. (2009), Intelligence, 37(1), 1–10.

terms.definition: Actions by school psychologists to promote the interests of students, families, and the profession at policy, systems, and community levels.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Model for Comprehensive and Integrated School Psychological Services (2020).

terms.definition: Clearly defined limits protecting the professional relationship; appropriate boundaries prevent dual relationships and maintain the integrity of professional services.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: Ongoing training, education, and learning activities undertaken to maintain and improve professional competence; an ethical obligation for school psychologists.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: Systematic assessment of a program's process and outcomes to determine whether it is effective and guide decisions about continuation, modification, or discontinuation.
Frequent, repeated assessment of academic or behavioral performance using validated tools (e.g., CBM) to determine whether an intervention is producing sufficient growth.
terms.citation: National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research. Deno, S. L. (1985), 'Curriculum-based measurement: The emerging alternative,' Exceptional Children, 52(3), 219–232.

terms.definition: Providing students, families, or staff with accurate information about psychological or educational topics (e.g., how anxiety works, what ADHD means) to support informed coping and decision-making.
Pertaining to the intersection of psychological and educational assessment and intervention; a psychoeducational evaluation assesses cognitive, academic, and social-emotional functioning.
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder; a DSM-5 diagnosis following trauma exposure, characterized by intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, and negative cognition/mood persisting over a month.
terms.citation: American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., 2013; text revision DSM-5-TR, 2022).
