terms.definition: Any consequence reducing the future probability of a behavior; can be positive (adding aversive stimulus) or negative (removing desired stimulus); generally less preferable than reinforcement-based approaches.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: The overrepresentation of students from racial minority groups in special education, gifted programs, or disciplinary actions beyond their proportion of the general school population.
terms.citation: IDEA disproportionality provisions, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.646–300.647; National Research Council, Donovan & Cross (Eds.) (2002), Minority Students in Special and Gifted Education.

terms.definition: The random placement of participants into experimental or control groups; the defining feature of a true experiment that eliminates systematic bias and allows causal inference.
The gold-standard experimental design using random assignment to treatment and control groups; provides the strongest evidence for causal claims about intervention effectiveness.
A relationship of mutual trust, respect, and openness between a professional and a client, consultee, or parent; essential for effective consultation, assessment, and counseling.
A standardized instrument using Likert-type response scales to measure behavioral, emotional, or adaptive functioning from the perspective of an informant.
Randomized Controlled Trial; see randomized controlled trial.
The ability to understand, interpret, and integrate the meaning of written text; dependent on decoding fluency, vocabulary knowledge, and background knowledge.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: The ability to read accurately, at an adequate rate, and with appropriate expression; bridges word-level decoding and text-level comprehension.
terms.citation: National Reading Panel (2000), Teaching Children to Read. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

terms.definition: Systematic examination of existing educational, medical, and psychological records to gather background information about a student; part of the RIOT framework (the R).
IDEA-required comprehensive re-evaluation of a student with a disability at least every three years to determine continued eligibility and current educational needs.
A counseling and consultation technique in which the listener paraphrases and reflects back the speaker's message to convey understanding and facilitate exploration.
A statistical technique modeling the relationship between predictor variables and an outcome; used to predict scores, control for variables, and test theoretical models.
The tendency for extreme scores on a first measurement to be less extreme on a second measurement; a statistical artifact and an internal validity threat in pre-post designs.
Any consequence that increases the future probability of the behavior it follows; can be positive (adding a desired stimulus) or negative (removing an aversive stimulus).
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Supportive services (speech-language therapy, counseling, transportation, occupational therapy) required to help a student with a disability benefit from special education.
The consistency and stability of test scores; a prerequisite for validity; includes test-retest (temporal), internal consistency, and interrater forms.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A numerical index (0 to 1.0) expressing the degree of reliability; values of .80 or above are generally considered adequate for high-stakes decisions.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: In consultation, a consultee's hesitancy or reluctance to implement recommended strategies; addressed through collaborative problem-solving, addressing concerns, and building rapport.
See RTI; an early intervention model using tiered instruction and frequent progress monitoring to identify students with learning disabilities; evolved into the broader MTSS framework.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.307–300.311 (permitting RTI in SLD identification); National Center on Response to Intervention (AIR).

terms.definition: A disciplinary philosophy focusing on repairing harm, restoring relationships, and rebuilding community rather than punitive consequences for rule violations.
terms.citation: International Institute for Restorative Practices (IIRP); Zehr, H. (2002). The Little Book of Restorative Justice. Good Books.

terms.definition: Proactive and responsive strategies (community-building circles, conferences) that build positive relationships and address conflict by involving affected parties in finding solutions.
terms.citation: International Institute for Restorative Practices (IIRP).

terms.definition: See grade retention; holding a student back a grade level due to insufficient academic progress; generally not supported by research as an effective long-term strategy.
terms.citation: Jimerson, S. R. (2001), 'Meta-analysis of grade retention research,' School Psychology Review, 30(3), 420–437.

terms.definition: In the RIOT framework, systematic examination of existing records (educational, medical, psychological) to collect background information about a student (the R in RIOT).
A data-collection framework categorizing assessment methods as Review, Interview, Observation, and Test; ensures comprehensive, multi-method, multi-informant evaluation.
Response to Intervention; a problem-solving model using tiered, data-driven instruction to identify students at risk, provide early intervention, and determine eligibility for special education.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.307–300.311 (permitting RTI in SLD identification); National Center on Response to Intervention (AIR).

terms.definition: A collaborative process creating a concrete plan for individuals at risk of suicide or self-harm, including warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts, and means restriction.
terms.citation: Stanley, B., & Brown, G. K. (2012), 'Safety Planning Intervention,' Cognitive and Behavioral Practice, 19(2), 256–264.

terms.definition: Vygotsky's concept of temporary, adjustable support (hints, modeling, prompting) provided by a more capable person to help a learner accomplish tasks within the ZPD; gradually faded as skill grows.
terms.citation: Term introduced by Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G. (1976), 'The role of tutoring in problem solving,' Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89–100; grounded in Vygotsky's ZPD (1978).

terms.definition: A derived score with a mean of 10 and standard deviation of 3, commonly used for cognitive and achievement test subtests; allows comparison across different subtests.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A graph displaying pairs of behavioral data across time periods; in behavioral assessment, used to identify patterns in when problem behavior occurs and potential antecedents.
The social, physical, and emotional quality of the school environment; positive school climate is linked to better academic achievement, attendance, and social-emotional wellbeing.
terms.citation: National School Climate Center; Thapa, A., et al. (2013), 'A review of school climate research,' Review of Educational Research, 83(3), 357–385.

terms.definition: Practices and policies protecting students and staff from harm; encompasses threat assessment, crisis planning, physical security, and social-emotional support systems.
The range of professional activities for which a practitioner has adequate training and supervised experience; ethical practice requires staying within this boundary.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: The range of professional activities a practitioner is authorized to perform based on training, licensure, certification, and role definition.
terms.citation: NASP Principles for Professional Ethics (2020); state licensure and certification statutes.

terms.definition: Giving meaning to assessment scores by comparing them to norms, applying confidence intervals, considering test reliability, and integrating with all available data.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A civil rights law (Rehabilitation Act) prohibiting discrimination based on disability in programs receiving federal funds; provides accommodations without requiring IDEA eligibility.
terms.citation: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794; 34 C.F.R. Part 104.

terms.definition: Social-Emotional Learning; evidence-based approaches to developing self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making.
terms.citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL), CASEL Framework (casel.org).

terms.definition: Intentional, non-suicidal injury to one's own body (e.g., cutting, burning); often functions as emotional regulation; requires careful assessment of intent, function, and safety.
A set of behavioral strategies (self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement) enabling students to regulate their own behavior with decreasing external support.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: A self-management strategy where students observe and record their own behavior or attention; increases awareness and has been shown to improve on-task behavior.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: The metacognitive ability to plan, monitor, and evaluate one's own learning strategies; students who self-regulate learn more effectively and independently.
terms.citation: Zimmerman, B. J. (2002), 'Becoming a self-regulated learner: An overview,' Theory Into Practice, 41(2), 64–70.

terms.definition: The capacity to manage emotions, attention, and behavior in adaptive, goal-directed ways; foundational for academic success and social competence.
Standard Error of Measurement; an estimate of the typical amount of random error in a test score; used to construct confidence intervals and interpret score differences.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A psychometric property of a screening tool; the proportion of individuals with the condition correctly identified as positive (true positive rate); high sensitivity minimizes false negatives.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Piaget's first cognitive stage (birth to age 2) in which infants develop knowledge through sensory experiences and motor actions; culminates in object permanence.
terms.citation: Piaget's theory of cognitive development; Piaget, J. (1952). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. International Universities Press.

terms.definition: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy; a strengths-based, short-term approach focused on building solutions and future goals rather than analyzing problems and their origins.
terms.citation: de Shazer, S. (1985). Keys to Solution in Brief Therapy. Norton; de Shazer & Berg.

terms.definition: A behavioral technique for building new, complex behaviors by reinforcing successive approximations to the target behavior; useful when the full behavior is not yet in the learner's repertoire.
terms.citation: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied Behavior Analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

terms.definition: Specific Learning Disability; an IDEA eligibility category covering disorders in one or more basic psychological processes affecting academic achievement in reading, math, or written expression.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10); SLD identification procedures, §§ 300.307–300.311.

terms.definition: The use of verbal and nonverbal communication in social contexts; impaired in autism spectrum disorder and social communication disorder.
The acquisition of social skills, prosocial behaviors, peer relationships, and understanding of social norms; shaped by family, peers, and culture.
The pursuit of equitable access to rights, resources, and opportunities, particularly for historically marginalized groups; an increasingly central value in school psychology ethics.
terms.citation: NASP Principles for Professional Ethics (2020); NASP position statements on social justice.

terms.definition: Advancing a student to the next grade level despite inadequate academic performance to avoid retention's social stigma; may perpetuate academic gaps if needs go unaddressed.
terms.citation: Jimerson, S. R. (2001), School Psychology Review, 30(3), 420–437 (research on retention and promotion).

terms.definition: Structured instruction in interpersonal skills (conversation, problem-solving, cooperation, emotional regulation); evidence-based for students with ASD, ADHD, and social-emotional difficulties.
Pertaining to the social and emotional dimensions of development and functioning, including relationship skills, emotional regulation, and empathy.
See SEL; a framework for explicitly teaching self-awareness, empathy, responsible decision-making, and relationship skills to improve student outcomes.
terms.citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL), CASEL Framework (casel.org).

terms.definition: See SFBT; a brief therapeutic model emphasizing client strengths, exceptions to problems, and concrete, achievable goals.
terms.citation: de Shazer, S. (1985). Keys to Solution in Brief Therapy. Norton; de Shazer & Berg.

terms.definition: The formal request initiating a comprehensive evaluation to determine whether a student qualifies for special education under IDEA; must be followed by evaluation within required timelines.
terms.citation: IDEA child find and evaluation provisions, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.111, 300.301.

terms.definition: See SLD; an IDEA disability category involving unexpected academic difficulty in reading, math, or written expression despite adequate intelligence and appropriate instruction.
terms.citation: IDEA, 34 C.F.R. § 300.8(c)(10); SLD identification procedures, §§ 300.307–300.311.

terms.definition: A psychometric property of a screening tool; the proportion of individuals without the condition correctly identified as negative (true negative rate); high specificity minimizes false positives.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Pertaining to communication through spoken language; speech-language pathologists address articulation, fluency, voice, and language disorders.
A measure of score variability indicating the average distance of scores from the mean; in most cognitive tests, the SD = 15 (mean = 100), so 1 SD above = 115.
See SEM; an index of score reliability indicating the typical random error in any single obtained score.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A derived score with a fixed mean (typically 100) and standard deviation (typically 15) that places performance in context of the norm group.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A finding that results are unlikely due to chance (typically p < .05); does not indicate effect size, practical importance, or the magnitude of the effect.
A situational phenomenon where awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group harms performance; relevant to standardized testing with students from stigmatized groups.
terms.citation: Steele, C. M., & Aronson, J. (1995), 'Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(5), 797–811.

terms.definition: The continuum of suicidal thoughts, communications, plans, and behaviors; requires prompt, structured risk assessment and safety planning.
terms.citation: Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS); Posner, K., et al. (2011), American Journal of Psychiatry, 168(12), 1266–1277.

terms.definition: Proactive schoolwide strategies including gatekeeper training, universal screening, means restriction, and crisis response planning to reduce student suicide risk.
terms.citation: SAMHSA Suicide Prevention Resource Center; American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.

terms.definition: The likelihood that an individual will engage in suicidal behavior; assessed through structured interviews examining ideation, plan, intent, means, and protective factors.
terms.citation: Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS); Posner, K., et al. (2011), American Journal of Psychiatry, 168(12), 1266–1277.

terms.definition: A comprehension strategy requiring identification and paraphrase of the main ideas of a text in condensed form; improves retention and supports academic writing.
Assessment conducted after instruction to evaluate overall learning and assign grades or make high-stakes decisions (e.g., end-of-year tests, state assessments).
A professional relationship in which a more experienced practitioner provides oversight, guidance, and feedback to a supervisee; governed by ethical standards in school psychology.
terms.citation: National Association of School Psychologists (NASP), Principles for Professional Ethics (2020).

terms.definition: Supports and services provided in general education settings to enable students with disabilities to be educated with non-disabled peers; part of the LRE continuum.
Temporary exclusion from school as a disciplinary consequence; subject to special protections under IDEA for students with disabilities, particularly beyond 10 cumulative days.
terms.citation: IDEA discipline procedures, 34 C.F.R. §§ 300.530–300.536.

terms.definition: A rigorous, structured literature synthesis using explicit, reproducible methods to identify, appraise, and synthesize all available evidence on a specific research question.
Structural, institutional, or policy-level obstacles preventing equitable access to resources and opportunities for marginalized groups; addressed through advocacy and systems change.
Planned, intentional efforts to alter organizational structures, policies, or practices at the school, district, or community level to improve outcomes for all students.
A derived score with a mean of 50 and standard deviation of 10; commonly used on behavior rating scales (e.g., BASC-3); scores ≥ 60–70 typically indicate clinical concern.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1976); established the 'duty to warn' — therapists must take reasonable steps to protect identifiable potential victims of credible threats.
terms.citation: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California, 17 Cal. 3d 425, 551 P.2d 334 (1976).

terms.definition: Tier 2 support; supplemental, evidence-based instruction for students not adequately responding to Tier 1; typically small group and more frequent than universal support.
terms.citation: MTSS Tier 2; Center on PBIS (pbis.org).

terms.definition: In the RIOT framework, standardized or norm-referenced measures yielding direct performance data about a student's abilities, achievement, or behavior.
A reliability measure of temporal stability; the correlation between scores from two administrations of the same test at different times; important for progress monitoring tools.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: The dynamic assessment format in which a baseline is measured, brief mediated instruction is provided, and the student is re-assessed to measure responsiveness to instruction.
terms.citation: Dynamic assessment; Lidz, C. S. (1987). Dynamic Assessment. Guilford Press.

terms.definition: A structured, multidisciplinary process for evaluating the seriousness of a threat to determine the appropriate safety and supportive response.
terms.citation: U.S. Secret Service National Threat Assessment Center (NTAC); Cornell, D. G., Comprehensive School Threat Assessment Guidelines (CSTAG).

terms.definition: A multidisciplinary school team (administrator, psychologist, counselor, law enforcement) trained to evaluate threats and coordinate appropriate safety and intervention responses.
terms.citation: U.S. Secret Service National Threat Assessment Center (NTAC); Cornell, D. G., Comprehensive School Threat Assessment Guidelines (CSTAG).

terms.definition: Universal, whole-school or whole-class core instruction and supports provided to all students; the foundation of MTSS; approximately 80% of students should respond adequately.
terms.citation: MTSS/PBIS framework; Center on PBIS (pbis.org).

terms.definition: Targeted, supplemental intervention for the approximately 15% of students who do not adequately respond to Tier 1; typically small-group, evidence-based, and more frequent.
terms.citation: MTSS/PBIS framework; Center on PBIS (pbis.org).

terms.definition: Intensive, individualized intervention for the approximately 5% of students not responding to Tier 1 and 2 supports; most data-intensive level; may include special education referral.
terms.citation: MTSS/PBIS framework; Center on PBIS (pbis.org); National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research.

terms.definition: A behavioral system in which students earn tokens for target behaviors that are later exchanged for preferred backup reinforcers; effective for increasing appropriate classroom behavior.
terms.citation: Ayllon, T., & Azrin, N. H. (1968). The Token Economy: A Motivational System for Therapy and Rehabilitation. Appleton-Century-Crofts; Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020).

terms.definition: An IDEA-required IEP component for students aged 16+ (or younger per state) that coordinates services supporting post-secondary education, employment, and independent living goals.
A psychological response to an overwhelming event that exceeds an individual's ability to cope; can have lasting effects on development, learning, behavior, and mental health.
A practice approach recognizing the pervasive effects of trauma and integrating this awareness into systems, policies, and services to prevent re-traumatization.
terms.citation: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) (2014). SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach.

terms.definition: The degree to which an intervention is implemented consistently and correctly as designed; also called implementation fidelity; essential for valid outcome attribution.
A screening result correctly identifying someone who has the target condition; the desired outcome in early identification efforts.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: Universal Design for Learning; a proactive instructional framework providing flexible means of representation, expression, and engagement to address diverse learner needs from the outset.
terms.citation: Universal design for learning, defined at 20 U.S.C. § 1003(24) (Higher Education Opportunity Act of 2008); CAST (cast.org), UDL Guidelines.

terms.definition: See UDL; a framework for designing instruction that is flexible and accessible for all learners, reducing the need for individual accommodations after the fact.
terms.citation: Universal design for learning, defined at 20 U.S.C. § 1003(24) (Higher Education Opportunity Act of 2008); CAST (cast.org), UDL Guidelines.

terms.definition: Tier 1 support; evidence-based instruction and prevention programs delivered to all students regardless of risk level.
terms.citation: MTSS Tier 1; Center on PBIS (pbis.org).

terms.definition: Brief, low-cost assessments administered to all students at regular intervals to identify those at risk for academic or social-emotional difficulties before they become severe.
terms.citation: National Center on Intensive Intervention (intensiveintervention.org), American Institutes for Research.

terms.definition: The degree to which a test accurately measures what it claims to measure and supports appropriate interpretations; validity is the most fundamental characteristic of any assessment tool.
terms.citation: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education, Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014).

terms.definition: A measure of the spread of scores calculated as the average of squared deviations from the mean; the square of the standard deviation; used in many statistical analyses.
Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales; a standardized, norm-referenced assessment of adaptive behavior across communication, daily living skills, socialization, and motor domains.
terms.citation: Sparrow, S. S., Cicchetti, D. V., & Saulnier, C. A., Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (Vineland-3, 2016). Pearson.

terms.definition: The brain's ability to interpret and use visual information; deficits can affect letter/word recognition in reading and spatial reasoning in mathematics.
Lev Vygotsky; Russian psychologist emphasizing the social context of learning, the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), and scaffolding; influential in dynamic assessment and instruction.
terms.citation: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in Society: The Development of Higher Psychological Processes. Harvard University Press.

terms.definition: Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children; one of the most widely used cognitive tests for children ages 6–16; yields a Full Scale IQ, Index scores, and subtest scores.
terms.citation: Wechsler, D., Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-V, 2014). Pearson.

terms.definition: Woodcock-Johnson Tests; a comprehensive battery of cognitive ability and academic achievement tests widely used in psychoeducational evaluations.
terms.citation: Schrank, F. A., McGrew, K. S., & Mather, N., Woodcock-Johnson IV (2014). Riverside Insights.

terms.definition: The ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information while performing a cognitive task; a core executive function strongly predictive of academic performance.
terms.citation: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974), 'Working memory,' in The Psychology of Learning and Motivation; Baddeley, A. (2000).

terms.definition: An individualized, collaborative planning process for students with complex needs that coordinates services across family, school, and community systems.
terms.citation: National Wraparound Initiative; Bruns, E. J., & Walker, J. S. (2010). The Resource Guide to Wraparound.

terms.definition: Comprehensive, coordinated services provided across multiple systems (school, mental health, social services, juvenile justice) for students and families with complex or multiple needs.
terms.citation: National Wraparound Initiative; Bruns, E. J., & Walker, J. S. (2010). The Resource Guide to Wraparound.

terms.definition: A standardized score indicating how many standard deviations above or below the mean a raw score falls; z = 0 is the mean; z = +1 is one standard deviation above the mean.
Vygotsky's concept describing the range of tasks a learner can perform with guidance but not independently; the optimal instructional target, addressed through scaffolding.
terms.citation: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in Society: The Development of Higher Psychological Processes. Harvard University Press.
